Maladaptive Strategies.value: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Any form of physical contact with others

Negative Appraisals.value: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal of feared uncontrollable rage is not well supported by the rest of the profile. There are no corresponding trigger, threat, memory, or strategy items suggesting anger-driven reactivity, aggression risk, or conflict; the other appraisals instead center on shame and hopelessness after rape. This makes the rage item clinically discordant within the selected five components.

issues.item: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
issues.explanation: The strategy of constant socialising is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile in this rape-related presentation. The selected triggers are solitary/sensory reminders (silence, outdoor smells, anniversary), and the appraisals are shame, suicidality, and feared rage. Constantly surrounding oneself with people does not connect clearly to these reminders and is somewhat at odds with body shame after rape, making it the least coherent avoidance/coping item here.

vignette: On the day that changed her life, Mabel was 54 and was cutting grass in the late afternoon light of the family farm. A man she had known for years slipped into her field, pressed her to the dirt and forced her into a violation that left her body and mind trembling. The moment she burst through the fence and sprinted into the scrub, the scent of loam and wet earth still clung to her skin. Years later, the faint smell of soil that the wind carries after a rainstorm in the fields now erupts in her, dragging the night‑time memory of that darkness into her present. In that instant the trigger of earth’s odor pulls her into a cascade of avoidance: she refuses to step foot in the same patch of ground, to be anywhere near the same level of ground in her mind, and she convinces herself that she must think only positive thoughts as a shield. The same smell, however, pulls her to a deeper belief that her life no longer holds meaning—she insists that the event has ruined everything she holds dear. The sense that her body has been dishonored, that the act has tainted her, makes the anniversary of the rape feel like a looming thunderclap. She feels shame in the quiet moments, and the silence in the early dawn on the farm when the machines are idle acts as a reminder that the world has not moved on. These negative appraisals—life not worth living, body shame, contamination—fuel her urge to keep away from any circumstance that reminds her of that day. She avoids being touched, even a casual pat on the shoulder, and she turns her back on any activity that might bring her back into the dark corners of her mind. When she senses even a single hush during the harvest, the absence of sound becomes a trigger that tells her that the threat is again present, and her appraisal that her life is meaningless is reinforced. In the days that followed, Mabel’s coping became a paradox. She told the farmhand who kept the fields together that she “has to think positive thoughts, to keep the bad ideas away.” By refusing to let herself feel anything but optimism, she actually strengthens her sense that the world is cruel and that her life is worthless. The act of forcing a positive frame becomes a trigger in itself: each time she tries to rewrite her thoughts, the memory of that violation flares, and the contamination she feels grows sharper. Her avoidance of being in the dark or being touched keeps her in a loop where the mind stays constantly on high alert, looking for the slightest echo of the event. The more she removes herself from touch and from the smell of earth, the more her appraisal that her body is tainted and her belief that nothing matters are deepened. Now 74, Mabel is still the backbone of the family farm, but she keeps the tractors at a distance, shuns the quiet of the barns, and has stopped allowing her partner, Kofi, to hold her hands during their evening conversations. The isolation has led to restless nights and a sense that she has become a ghost in her own home. When Kofi asked her why she would not let him touch her arm, she could only say, “I feel dirty, and I don’t want to bring that into our lives.” Her fear that the shame will seep into the next generation made her even more reluctant to discuss her trauma, and she finally found herself on the porch one rain‑shrouded afternoon, listening to the distant rumble of the old tractor and realizing she could no longer keep living in the echo of that day. The decision to seek help came after Kofi’s patient insistence that she could not be her own “captive.” Mabel is now afraid that the process will unravel the last thread of control she has held and hopes to regain a sense that her life still has meaning beyond the soil she once feared.
